source: Pereira, Correa, Meneguzzi, Seipp (2026) LeanPlan: Optimal Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics and Admissibility Proofs
finding: A coding agent (GPT-5.6 Sol) wrote a domain heuristic plus a Lean 4 proof that it never overestimates. With these heuristics, A* solved more tasks than Scorpion's best config. The proof is checked by machine, so the guarantee does not depend on the model being right.
numbers: 13 domains (10 IPC 2023 + 3 new, unreleased), 90 test tasks each, 1170 tasks. Total solved: blind Scorpion 166, blind LeanPlan 162, Scorpion LM-cut 209, Scorpion SCP 272, LeanPlan 348. IPC 2023 sum: LM-cut 198, SCP 221, LeanPlan 281. New domains: SCP 51, LeanPlan 67. Spanner is the biggest gain (derived from the paper's sums: LeanPlan 72 vs SCP 30, a dead-end test); without Spanner LeanPlan 209 vs SCP 191. SCP beats LeanPlan in 4 IPC domains.
quote: first planning system to find optimal plans with LLM-generated heuristics whose admissibility is machine-checked
limits: One LLM and one agent harness. A heuristic is accepted only if it solves at least as many training tasks as Scorpion and expands fewer states. Domain assumptions are checked per task: the certificate refused 3 of 1170 test tasks (all Cisterns), which count as unsolved. Optimal A* search, unlike the satisficing papers. Per-domain cells were read from a scrambled table layout; sums were used to cross-check.
agent_relevance: Shows a code-verified model proposal can keep a hard guarantee. Pattern for us: model proposes a scorer, code checks a stated property on every instance, refuse to use the scorer when the check fails.

source: Pereira et al. (2026) LeanPlan, sections 5.2 and 5.3: generalisation beyond training size and dead ends
finding: The generated heuristics matter most on tasks bigger than the training tasks. A heuristic that ignores interactions between objects loses where those interactions matter (Sokoban). A dead-end test gave the largest single jump.
numbers: Of 595 IPC 2023 test tasks with more objects than any training task of their domain: LeanPlan solves 53, Scorpion SCP 13. On the 211 tasks both solve, LeanPlan expands fewer states on 152 and more on 55. Versus blind LeanPlan, expansions fall by more than two orders of magnitude in total. IPC hard tasks have 2.5x to 57x the objects of training tasks; new-domain test tasks at most about 2x.
limits: The authors say the Sokoban loss is presumably because SCP abstractions capture box interactions that LeanPlan's relaxations ignore (their wording; not tested). Counts compare whole configurations, not heuristics alone.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 3: a scorer that drops an interaction is weak exactly where that interaction decides the result, and a cheap dead-end check recovers a lot. Our scorer should include explicit must-not-fail tests.

source: Meneguzzi, Buchweitz, Correa, Putrich, Pereira (2026) Hierarchical Task Network Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics
finding: The Correa et al. recipe (generate code heuristics, select on training, search) transfers to HTN planning. The single best model's heuristic matched the virtual best over five models, so the multi-model portfolio added nothing in coverage.
numbers: 139 problems, 6 HTN domains. Solved: PANDA RCFF 134, RCLMCut 113, TDG 117, LMCOUNT 118, Claude Opus 4 heuristic (CO4) 131, LLM virtual best of 5 models 131. Fewer expansions than PANDA on 83% of shared problems. Median expansions: Opus 4 1878, Gemini 3 Flash 4346, Gemini 3 Pro 14746, Gemini 2.0 Flash about 48600, Gemini 2.5 Pro about 51200 (best to worst about 27x). Robot domain: LLM 12 vs PANDA 20.
limits: Coverage is a virtual best over GBFS, A* and WA*, which favours the LLM columns. The selection instance (smallest problem per domain) is also in the evaluation set, though every system solves all six. Only 5 of 9 models enter the main table.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and gap 7: model choice matters more than search choice (27x spread), and a 5-model portfolio did not beat the best single model on coverage. Samples across models were not additive here.

source: Meneguzzi et al. (2026) HTN heuristics, section 5.3 failure accounting and selection rule
finding: Many generated scorers do not even run. Selection used one cheap rule: run each candidate on the smallest training instance and keep the one with fewest expanded nodes (ties to the shorter plan).
numbers: 780 candidate heuristics in total over the nine models and six domains. 419 passed the selection filter; 361 were rejected (parse error, exception, timeout). Of the 419 deployed, 347 solved at least one problem and 72 broke on every problem; 60 of those 72 (83%) assumed the wrong state type (bitwise integers). Four models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, GPT-5.2) got a surviving candidate in only one domain each.
limits: Single training instance for selection, so the rule is cheap but its quality versus a larger training set is not compared. Authors did not retry failed prompts, to avoid selection bias. Default sampling temperature only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 and gap 4: a validity and smallest-instance filter removed 46% of candidates before any test. The cost of writing and testing scorers is real; budget a repair step and a schema check for the scorer interface.

source: Gestrin and Seipp (2026) LLM-Evolved Domain-Independent Heuristics for Symbolic AI Planning (LM4Plan, ICAPS 2026)
finding: An LLM evolved C++ heuristics in a MAP-Elites archive. The best one beat every hand-made domain-independent heuristic on unseen domains. Starting from the trivial blind heuristic gave a higher ceiling than starting from FF, and the best result was itself an FF-like heuristic.
numbers: Test set: 8 held-out IPC 2023 Learning Track domains, 720 tasks, 30 min and 8 GB, greedy search. Best evolved heuristic solved 368 of 720 vs 352 for the strongest baseline (hadd). Blind-seeded scores 0.528 to 0.606; FF-seeded 0.543 to 0.586; 3 of 9 blind-seeded runs beat every FF-seeded run. First-attempt working heuristic 79.1%; one repair 13.3%; failed after 4 attempts 2.5%. Reasoning effort none to medium: initial success 73.0% to 83.4%; scores above zero about unchanged. API spend about $16 (none), $24 (low), $33 (medium) per run.
quote: the best blind-seeded heuristic is itself an FF-variant
limits: Three open-weight models (GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6, MiMo-v2.5-pro). The gain of 16 tasks over 720 is small and run-to-run variance is large. Greedy search is unfavourable to the admissible baselines, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and gap 7: the useful output of the models was a known relaxation (FF-like) rediscovered, and diversity of starting points mattered more than a strong seed. For us: keep a pool of different relaxations, not one polished one.

source: Pereira, Correa, Seipp (2026) Property-Guided LLM Program Synthesis for Planning
finding: Instead of ranking 25 sampled scorers by a score, check a formal property on training data and feed the first counterexample back to the model. This used about 7 times fewer generations and about 1000 times less evaluation, and solved more test tasks. Selecting by training score (sample-and-select) did badly when search was limited to hill climbing.
numbers: 10 IPC 2023 domains, 900 test tasks, out-of-distribution sizes. Hill climbing (no search) with property-guided heuristics: 623.3 tasks (mean of 3 runs). Sample-and-select (re-run with Gemini 3.1 Pro) with GBFS: 573; the same heuristics under hill climbing: 430. FF with GBFS 298; FF under hill climbing 30. Generations: 101 candidates over 30 runs, 3.4 per run (SD 3.0) vs 25 fixed. Evaluation: 10.75 minutes per domain vs 206.25 CPU-hours reported by Correa et al.
limits: The property is 'every state reached by improving moves has an improving successor', checked on training tasks; the authors say counterexamples on test tasks remain possible. The baseline CPU-hours are quoted from the earlier paper, not re-measured. Needs a verifiable property, which PDDL has and free text may not.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and gap 10: ranking by training score at fixed cost is beaten by a repair loop using a checkable property. Charge for the 25-sample selection. Our scorer should come with a property we can test, not only a pass rate.

source: Debnath, Adedigba, Mallipeddi (2026) When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability
finding: The delete-relaxation estimate h_add ranks held-out instances by true optimal plan length far better than learned alternatives, with no training. It is a rank signal for difficulty, which is the property a relaxed solve must have to be useful for ranking.
numbers: Held-out domains Blocksworld, Logistics, Mystery-Blocksworld, N = 126, 164, 133 BFS-solved instances. Spearman |rho| with optimal plan length: h_add 0.894, 0.976, 0.923 (mean 0.931); ridge on structure 0.707; object count 0.657; ARC retrieval model 0.400. Re-simulating 1,006 saved plans gave zero failures. On Logistics h_add and goal count are indistinguishable.
limits: Correlates with the optimal plan length of small BFS-solved instances (object counts 2 to 9). It does not measure LLM success and does not rank children inside one search. Seven STRIPS domains, one LLM (Qwen 2.5-72B) for the success tests. These domains are not dead-end heavy.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, partly: a relaxed estimate ranks problem difficulty well when no constraint is lethal. Still not the test we need (relaxed rank vs real result of a candidate), so K22 stays open.

source: Debnath et al. (2026), section 6.2 predicate renaming
finding: Renaming symbols while keeping the transition system identical cuts a model's valid-plan rate, with no change in refusals. The loss comes from malformed and inapplicable actions.
numbers: Qwen 2.5-72B, 40 BFS-solved Blocksworld instances. Valid-plan success by fraction renamed: 0% 67.5% (CI 52.0 to 79.9); 25% 62.5%; 50% 47.5%; 75% 37.5%; 100% 40.0% (CI 26.3 to 55.4). Refusal rate 0% at every level. Not monotone step to step (N = 40).
limits: One model, one domain, N = 40; the endpoint intervals barely overlap. Direct plan writing, not scorer writing.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and gap 9: part of apparent skill is vocabulary. Our check: run each relaxed-solve step on a renamed copy and compare. If the result changes, the model is relying on recall.

finding: A structural score that ranks well does not by itself tell which instances the model will solve. A threshold calibrated on 140 real model outcomes did far better than any zero-shot score.
numbers: 100 sampled instances per domain, Qwen 2.5-72B. Zero-shot routing correct: 23% to 73% (best, ARC-ZS 73 on Blocksworld; Logistics at or below 50). With 140 calibration outcomes: ARC-FS 99, 99, 100; object-count 86, 77, 85; goal count 64 everywhere. Static and Oracle both 100% because a symbolic fallback always succeeds. h_add was not run in routing (the authors flag it as an extension).
limits: The table measures separation of likely-succeed from likely-fail at one threshold, not ranking inside a search. The paper itself says routing quality should not be assumed to track ranking quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a relaxed rank must be calibrated against the full candidate's real test outcome per problem class. Log the pair (relaxed score, real result) and refit the threshold.

source: Sharon (2026) Tree of Thoughts as a Classical Heuristic Search Problem (SoCS 2026)
finding: A taxonomy of LLM tree search in classical terms. LLM-given h-values are fitted or prompted, not derived from domain knowledge or relaxations, so admissibility and consistency do not apply. A comparative judgement over siblings gives only an order, which cannot be added to path cost or used to rank nodes from different parents.
numbers: No new experiments. Notes that Correa et al. 2025 showed LLMs can write external heuristic functions, and lists ways to regain guarantees: a closed-form admissible heuristic as a floor, pathmax for consistency, approximation bounds.
limits: Survey and taxonomy; claims are about the literature as read by the author, not measured. Absence of relaxation-based LLM h-values is the author's reading of the field.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and gap 4: no ToT work in this survey uses a self-made relaxed solve for h. Design rule for S3: if the model rates siblings, ranks are valid only inside one parent's set; a code-computed score can compare across parents.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Learn to Relax with Large Language Models: AutoCO (ACL 2026), ablation and effectiveness sections
finding: In constraint optimisation, letting the LLM weight each constraint's importance and set how far to relax it (inside generated search code) beat both no relaxation and an expert-set relaxation. Removing the relaxation module hurt about as much as removing the other main modules.
numbers: SFL-8 success: original constraints plateau at 52%, AutoCO reaches 80% (+28 points; 1.1x over the expert strategy at 2500 iterations). SFL-5 (Dual): AutoCO 53%, +25 points over no relaxation. Ablation, optimality-gap increase versus full method: without relaxation +21.55%, without 3-step generation +14.10%, without MCTS +17.46%, without bidirectional coevolution +23.73% (averages).
limits: Numeric optimisation problems, not text puzzles. The LLM both picks which constraint to relax and how much; no arm compares the model's pick with a systematic code enumeration, so gap 2 is not answered.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: shows the amount of relaxation is tunable and model-set values help, but not whether enumerating constraints by code is better. Keep the test: drop each stated constraint in turn by code vs model pick, at equal tokens.

source: Malek et al. (Google DeepMind, 2025) Frontier LLMs Still Struggle with Simple Reasoning Tasks (Unpuzzles), Tables 1 and 3
finding: Simplified versions of famous puzzles are solved worse than the originals because the model answers the memorised original. Rewriting the simple version in new surface context (same logic) recovers much of the loss. So a renamed copy is a cheap detector of the pull to memory.
numbers: Table 1 (97 items), puzzle vs unpuzzle correct %: Gemini 1.5 79.4 vs 17.5; Gemini 2.0 Flash 78.4 vs 38.1; Gemini 2.5 Pro 93.8 vs 62.9; Claude 3.7 77.3 vs 48.5; GPT-4o 75.3 vs 19.6; o1 86.7 vs 59.8; o3 87.6 vs 74.2; R1 87.6 vs 59.8. Table 3 (64 items), unpuzzle vs context-shifted %: Gemini 2.0F 53 vs 70; Gemini 2.0F Thinking 36 vs 48; GPT-4o 33 vs 52; o1 50 vs 59; o3 75 vs 80; R1 67 vs 73; Claude 3.7 55 vs 63. Context corruption (answer copies the original) in 80 of 97 solutions for Gemini 1.5 and 34 for Gemini 2.5 Pro.
limits: The 64-item subset has numeric or categorical answers. Context-shifting was done by a model prompt with a structure check. Human annotators judged correctness. It shows renaming helps; it does not show renaming catches every case. The task here is answering a trivial puzzle, not using a simplification to guide search.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a re-contexted copy of the simple problem raised accuracy for every model tested, so a renamed-variant check is a usable detector (drop on original wording, gain on shifted). It is a signal, not proof the model is not leaning on memory.

source: Correa, Pereira, Seipp (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics, cost accounting (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Writing a scorer once per domain was cheaper in calls and money than asking the same model for a plan per task, and it solved more. Selection was by training tasks.
numbers: Total API cost for all heuristics: DeepSeek V3 $0.25, R1 $6.12. End-to-end plan generation: V3 $2.79, R1 $13.62. 200 calls (25 heuristics x 8 domains) vs 720 calls (90 tasks x 8 domains). R1 end-to-end takes days; heuristics a few hours. R1 plans solved 174; R1 heuristics 373.
limits: This compares code-scorer vs direct full plan, not code-scorer vs a model rating children inside search. Generation cost excludes the CPU cost of running GBFS on 25 candidates (206.25 CPU-hours per domain as quoted by d06). Gemini models used free API access.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the large cost is the CPU search used for selection, not tokens. In a text setting with no executable instances, the model is also the evaluator, so test and selection cost must be charged to the token budget.

source: Correa et al. (2025), memorisation vs reasoning: Spanner variant, obfuscated Blocksworld, Rod-Rings
finding: Three recall tests. A changed Spanner domain (spanners no longer break) got a perfect heuristic. Random renaming cost the R1 heuristic about 40% of its Blocksworld coverage. A never-released domain nearly matched hFF.
numbers: Obfuscated Blocksworld: R1 heuristic 66 solved vs 40 obfuscated; hFF 27 vs 28. Rod-Rings (unreleased): o3 heuristic 58 vs hFF 59 tasks. Spanner variant: best heuristic gave optimal plan lengths for all states.
limits: One model per test (R1 for renaming, o3 for Rod-Rings). No repeat runs reported for obfuscation. The authors call obfuscation highly adversarial for LLMs.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: LeanPlan (d01, three unreleased domains, 67 vs SCP 51) and Gestrin and Seipp (d05, held-out domains) add independent evidence on new domains with other models, but renamed-domain evidence still rests on this one obfuscation run. K13 gains a second source on new domains, not on renaming.

source: Bukkapatnam and Karuturi (2026) LM-Landmarks: Language Model Guided Landmark Generation for Classical Planning with Formal Soundness Guarantees (ICML 2026 LM4Plan), listing page
finding: Abstract only. The PDF was not reachable (OpenReview showed a check page). The model proposes landmarks; a delete-relaxation test verifies each before use; the authors claim soundness and admissibility proofs and a node reduction.
numbers: 8 IPC domains, Fast Downward. Coverage +7.5 points over FF and +3.1 over LAMA. Search nodes down 41% vs FF and 37% vs LAMA, no loss of plan optimality. Claimed bound: expected expansions fall by a factor of order R times kappa (recall times average landmark cost; the abstract's notation is inconsistent).
limits: No arm without verification is reported in the abstract, so gap 8 (verified vs unverified proposals) is NOT answered. No per-domain table, task count or number of proposals seen. Workshop poster.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. The design is sound: accept only proposals that pass a check. Add our own unverified arm to measure what verification buys.

source: Gestrin and Seipp (2026), section 5.3: evolved heuristics and memorised FF
finding: The strongest evolved heuristic was an FF-style relaxation plus corrective penalties and a reset mechanism. It came from a blind seed with no FF code shown, so the models already knew FF. Reasoning effort raised the chance of a working program, not its quality.
numbers: Best heuristic (evolved-blind-medium-2): FF-style hFF plus two corrective penalties (a per-unachieved-goal penalty min(hadd(g), hFF) and a further term) and an efficient reset, 368 of 720 test tasks vs 352 for hadd. Reasoning effort none to medium: zero-score heuristics fall, scores above zero about unchanged.
limits: The authors infer memorisation from the FF rediscovery; it is an inference, not a test. Three open-weight models. Trajectories cluster by run rather than by effort level.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 5: the helpful design was a relaxation plus explicit penalties for what relaxation misses (goal-by-goal penalty, reset). For us: pair any relaxed score with a short list of must-pass checks, and expect the model to recall classic relaxations.
